say.text: A 2-year-old with known TOF cries hard, then turns deeply blue and limp. You have seconds, and I haven't taught you the steps yet.
Your very first move?

choices.label: IV furosemide to offload the heart
A vasodilator to ease the strain

say.text: Think about which way the blood is choosing to go. What could you do to the systemic side to make that route less attractive?

Tempting: a limp, blue, distressed child looks like heart failure. But the spell steps aim at resistance, filling and the pulmonary side, not diuresis. IV fluid boluses, for example, improve RV filling.
The first move is knee-chest positioning, to increase systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause here: treating the spell like congestion would drain the very filling the RV needs.

say.text: Tempting: lower resistance, ease the strain. But that is the wrong direction. Knee-chest positioning works by increasing systemic vascular resistance, and phenylephrine later does the same job by increasing systemic afterload.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note this reversal: every resistance step in a spell pushes systemic resistance up, never down.

say.text: Yes: knee-chest positioning, to increase systemic vascular resistance. Crying is a classic agitation trigger, and spells need a rapid and aggressive approach.
You just raised resistance on one side. Now try the rest of the problem.
Still blue after knee-chest. Choose the pair of steps where both reasons make sense.

choices.label: Oxygen (pulmonary vasodilation) and IV fluid bolus (RV filling)
Oxygen and a vasodilator to drop systemic resistance

say.text: One step opens the pulmonary side. One step gives the right ventricle more to fill with. Neither lowers systemic resistance.
Tempting: diuretic plus vasodilator is the failing-heart reflex. But a spell calls for IV fluid boluses to improve RV filling, and for increasing systemic resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read: fluids in, resistance up. The reverse of the heart-failure reflex.

say.text: Oxygen is right: it causes pulmonary vasodilation. The vasodilator is the trap. Lowering systemic resistance sends even more blood across the VSD the wrong way; the aim is to increase systemic afterload.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep half of that answer (oxygen) and flip the other half.

say.text: Yes. Oxygen, to cause pulmonary vasodilation. IV fluid boluses, to improve RV filling.
Your picks fit one logic: open the lungs, fill the RV, raise the systemic side.
Still not settling. Which drug directly increases systemic afterload?
Afterload is the resistance the left ventricle pumps against. Which drug here is a pressor that raises it?
Tempting: it is in the spell toolkit. But its job is different: IV beta-blockers decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further. The afterload drug is IV phenylephrine.
Tempting: it is also in the toolkit. But morphine is a sedative given during a spell. The afterload drug is IV phenylephrine, to increase systemic afterload.
Yes: IV phenylephrine, to increase systemic afterload.
The others each have their own job: beta-blockers slow the heart and aid RV filling, and morphine sedates.
The spell settles. Before I teach repair: when would you do complete surgical repair?

choices.label: Immediately in every child; the matter is settled
After the first 3 months, though timing is debated

say.text: Ask yourself: is the timing a settled rule, or an open argument? Then think about what StatPearls describes.
Tempting: sick child, fix it now. But the timing of repair is still in debate, and StatPearls describes deferring complete repair to after the first 3 months.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the word to remember is debated: no single settled answer.

say.text: Tempting: wait for a bigger child. But the timing is still in debate, and StatPearls describes deferring only until after the first 3 months, not years.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset the number: after the first 3 months, not adolescence.

say.text: Yes. The timing of repair is still in debate; StatPearls describes deferring complete repair to after the first 3 months of life.

choices.label: Go deeper: who gets which timing

say.text: Al Mosa et al. consider 3–6 months likely ideal for elective repair, advocating it in asymptomatic patients.
They prefer primary neonatal or early repair for symptomatic infants.
Staging with initial palliation is reserved for high-risk infants: low birth weight or prematurity, and small or discontinuous pulmonary arteries. Neonates without those features are not palliated.
Palliation has costs: a limited shunt lifespan, more late sudden death, and pulmonary artery stenosis and distortion.
When palliation is chosen, the Blalock-Taussig shunt is used. Which vessels does it connect?

choices.label: Subclavian artery to ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery
Aorta straight to the right ventricle
Subclavian artery to the superior vena cava

say.text: It borrows a branch of the aortic arch and sends blood toward the lungs. Which pair fits?
Tempting: more blood out of the aorta. But the shunt is not inside the heart. The Blalock-Taussig shunt connects the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.
Tempting: subclavian is right, and a vein sounds plausible. But the target is the lung's artery: the Blalock-Taussig shunt connects the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.
Yes: subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.
A child repaired years ago is back. What is the commonest reason to reoperate?
Think about what the surgeon had to rebuild to relieve the obstruction, and what that rebuilding does to the valve.
Tempting: the original holes should be the problem. But the commonest indication for reoperation is pulmonary insufficiency, a result of reconstructing the RVOT.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the problem after repair is a new one, caused by the repair itself.

say.text: Tempting: the old obstruction returns. But the commonest indication for reoperation is pulmonary insufficiency; pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-anchor: most common reoperation after repair is pulmonary insufficiency.

say.text: Yes. Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT, and pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.
Valve replacement can be done surgically or by a transcatheter approach.
Late problem: what proportion of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias?
It is common, but not universal. Think of a figure close to half.
Tempting: repair sounds curative. But 40–50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia.
Tempting: it feels like a big risk. But it is not everyone: 40–50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias.
Yes: 40–50%, including ventricular tachycardia. The risk of sudden death is 6–9% 30 years after the surgical procedure.
Flip it. With no surgery at all, which is the most frequent cause of death?
You managed one of these tonight at the bedside.
Tempting: chronic hypoxaemia does cause stroke. But strokes are 17% of deaths, behind hypoxic spells at 68%.
Tempting: cerebral abscess is a real complication. But brain abscesses are 13% of deaths, behind hypoxic spells at 68%.
Yes: hypoxic spells (68%), then cerebrovascular accidents (17%) and brain abscesses (13%).
Chronic hypoxaemia can cause hyperviscosity, abnormal haemostasis, stroke, cerebral abscess and endocarditis.
Last question on risk: who needs to think about endocarditis?

choices.label: Patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired

say.text: Does surgery switch the risk off?
Tempting: repair feels like a cure. But patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of endocarditis.
Yes: repaired or unrepaired, the endocarditis risk stays.
Back on the ward: another spell. Which pair of reasons is right?

choices.label: Knee-chest raises systemic resistance; phenylephrine raises systemic afterload
Knee-chest drains the lungs; furosemide offloads the heart

say.text: Both resistance steps push in the same direction on the systemic side.
Tempting: it echoes your first attempt. But knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance, and phenylephrine increases systemic afterload; fluids help RV filling.
Yes: both steps raise the systemic side, so blood is pushed through the lungs.
Tonight's order: position, oxygen, fluids, then phenylephrine.
